structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway reflecting on his father’s advice to reserve judgment, which shaped his tendency to absorb others’ confidences and ultimately led to his disillusionment after returning from the East, where he witnessed moral chaos and privileged excesses—except for Jay Gatsby, whose extraordinary gift for hope and romantic sensitivity set him apart. In the spring of 1922, Nick rents a modest eighty-dollar bungalow in West Egg, overlooking Long Island Sound, between two grand estates, including the mysterious mansion of Gatsby; after feeling isolated until a stranger asks him for directions, he drives by car to East Egg to visit his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whom he knew at Yale, where they live in a grand Georgian Colonial mansion with French windows open to the breeze. During dinner, Tom aggressively espouses racist pseudoscience from The Rise of the Coloured Empires, a phone call reveals his affair in New York, and Daisy, after retreating and returning with forced cheer, invents a story about a nightingale on the lawn before confiding in Nick that she wishes her daughter would be a 'beautiful little fool.' Later, as Nick leaves, he observes Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, stretching his arms toward a single green light across the bay, before vanishing into the night.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer afternoon, Nick Carraway accompanies Tom Buchanan by train to the valley of ashes, where Tom forcibly stops the train and drags Nick off to meet Myrtle Wilson, wife of the pale, spiritless George Wilson, beneath the looming eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg; Myrtle emerges from the run-down garage, dismisses her husband, and agrees to go to New York with Tom, purchasing a dog, perfume, and magazines before boarding a lavender taxicab with them; they arrive at Myrtle’s rented apartment on the top floor of a building at 158th Street, where she hosts a chaotic gathering with her sister Catherine and the McKees, drinking whisky and performing a haughty, pretentious persona amid cluttered furniture and a grotesque enlarged photograph of her mother; as the party descends into drunken revelry, Myrtle loudly shouts Daisy’s name, provoking Tom to violently break her nose with his open hand, after which she collapses bleeding on the couch while others scramble in confusion, Mr. McKee awakens dazedly and leaves, and Nick departs with him in the elevator, later finding himself exhausted in Pennsylvania Station at dawn waiting for a train.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: Nick Carraway receives a formal invitation to attend a lavish party at Jay Gatsby’s mansion on Long Island, arriving after seven p.m. by car amid a sea of guests transported by Rolls-Royce and station wagons, where he wanders among strangers overhearing wild rumors about Gatsby—such as that he killed a man or was a German spy—while observing extravagant details like five crates of fruit delivered weekly, a bar stocked with forgotten cordials, and an orchestra with a full pit. He meets Jordan Baker and encounters an inebriated man in the library who is astonished to discover Gatsby’s books are real, not cardboard props, and later connects with a war veteran who invites him to fly in a hydroplane the next morning, yet still has not met Gatsby. Eventually, Nick Carraway discovers that the host is Gatsby himself, who reveals a rare, reassuring smile, invites him to fly the next morning at nine o’clock, and stands apart from the party’s chaos as guests descend into disorder: a chorus girl weeps ink-stained tears, couples argue violently, and wives are carried off kicking; Jordan Baker is called away alone to speak with Gatsby for an hour, and the night ends with a car crash outside the gate involving Owl Eyes and another man, neither admitting to driving. As Nick Carraway departs, he sees Gatsby alone on the porch gesturing farewell under a faint moon, while the party’s noise fades into silence. In midsummer, Nick Carraway reflects on his daily life as a clerk in New York, lunching with colleagues in dark restaurants, studying investments at the Yale Club’s library while avoiding rowdy patrons, and walking home along Madison Avenue and Fifth Avenue, haunted by loneliness and romantic fantasies; he reconnects with Jordan Baker, initially drawn by her fame as a golf champion, but becomes troubled by her dishonesty—she lies about damaging a borrowed car and he recalls her scandalous tournament cheating involving a moved ball and retracted testimony—and their conversation about driving reveals her belief that others must avoid her, which he finds both troubling and compelling, though he remains emotionally restrained by his ongoing letters to a woman back home, whose image lingers with unsettling specificity, including the memory of her perspiration on her upper lip while playing tennis.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion erupts into chaotic opulence as guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York arrive by car, mingling amid cocktails and flowers while rumors swirl about Gatsby’s origins—including claims he is a bootlegger, related to Von Hindenburg, or even the devil. Nick Carraway recalls numerous eccentric attendees like Ripley Snell, who was run over by Mrs. Ulysses Swett’s car while drunk on the gravel drive, and Henry L. Palmetto, who later killed himself by jumping in front of a subway train, all of whom know nothing of Gatsby despite his lavish hospitality. In late July, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored nickel-accented car with a three-noted horn, inviting him to lunch; during the drive to Manhattan, Gatsby offers an elaborate, inconsistent personal history including Oxford, wartime heroism with a Montenegrin medal, and European decadence, while revealing he wants Nick Carraway to arrange a meeting with Jordan Baker about an undisclosed matter, later using a commissioner’s card to evade a traffic stop. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsheim, a crime figure with hair growing from his nostrils and cuff buttons made of human molars, who chillingly recounts the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and reveals Gatsby fixed the 1919 World Series, leaving Nick Carraway stunned; Gatsby abruptly departs to make a phone call, and Nick Carraway spots Tom Buchanan before realizing Gatsby has vanished. Flashing back to October 1917, Jordan Baker recalls seeing Daisy Fay in her white roadster with Lieutenant Jay Gatsby in Louisville, after which Daisy’s family prevented her from bidding him farewell, leading to her marriage to Tom Buchanan in June 1918 with a $350,000 pearl necklace—hours before the wedding, Jordan found Daisy drunk and weeping over a letter and the necklace, though she recovered with ammonia and ice and married Tom without hesitation. Finally, after leaving the Plaza, Jordan and Nick Carraway ride in a victoria through Central Park at dusk, where Jordan reveals Gatsby bought his mansion solely so Daisy could see the green light across the bay, and he now asks Nick Carraway to invite Daisy to tea so he can visit unseen, having spent years reading Chicago newspapers hoping to see her name; as they pass Fifty-Ninth Street, Nick Carraway draws Jordan closer, captivated by her poise, and reflects on the phrase: 'There are only the pursued, the pursuing, the busy, and the tired.'

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night, Nick returns to his West Egg home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but empty, with only wind causing the lights to flicker; Gatsby approaches him, awkwardly offering a business opportunity tied to Wolfsheim, which Nick declines. The next morning, Nick invites Daisy to tea, warning her not to bring Tom, and as heavy rain floods the estate, Gatsby sends a gardener to mow Nick’s lawn and delivers an entire greenhouse of flowers. Daisy arrives by large open car with chauffeur Ferdie, and Gatsby enters the house pale and trembling, nearly knocking over a mantelpiece clock; after an excruciating silence, Daisy cries and Gatsby radiates joy, inviting her to tour his mansion. They walk via the road and enter through the big postern, where Daisy admires the estate’s gardens—filled with jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate—but finds the interior eerily silent. Gatsby shows her opulent rooms including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons, interrupting Mr. Klipspringer doing liver exercises in pajamas, before throwing dozens of luxurious shirts—linen, silk, flannel—in vivid colors and monograms onto the floor, causing Daisy to sob overwhelmed by their beauty. As rain resumes, Gatsby points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, acknowledging its symbolic collapse now that she is present; he shows her photographs of Mr. Dan Cody and himself as a young man in yachting attire, and they examine newspaper clippings about her until interrupted by a phone call about a misinterpreted business location. Daisy marvels at pink and golden clouds over the Sound, whimsically wishing to put Gatsby inside one, and Gatsby summons Klipspringer to play sentimental piano songs while they sit in shadowed isolation; Nick observes Gatsby’s face regain bewilderment as he realizes Daisy cannot fulfill his idealized vision, and as he departs, he sees Gatsby clutching Daisy’s hand, utterly absorbed in her voice, having forgotten his presence entirely.

structure.title: VI
structure.summary: A New York reporter arrives at Gatsby’s mansion seeking a statement, misled by rumors that Gatsby is connected to an underground pipeline to Canada or lives in a boat disguised as a house; the narrative then traces Gatsby’s origins as James Gatz of North Dakota, who, at seventeen, rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht, the Tuolomee, anchored off Lake Superior, and began working for Cody in multiple roles—steward, mate, skipper, secretary, and jailor—over five years of transcontinental travel, absorbing wealth and sophistication until Ella Kaye seized Cody’s fortune, leaving Gatsby with only his newly forged identity; later, after a weeks-long absence, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled by the unexpected arrival of Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit on horseback, who politely decline Gatsby’s offer of drinks and supper despite his eager hospitality, with Sloane explicitly preventing Gatsby from joining them for dinner as they depart on horseback just as Gatsby emerges prepared to follow in his car; later that week, Tom and Daisy attend one of Gatsby’s parties, where Daisy is charmed by celebrity faces but deeply unsettled by the raw energy and moral looseness of West Egg, prompting Gatsby to confide in Nick Carraway his desperate hope that Daisy will declare she never loved Tom, so they can repeat the past and restore their relationship to how it was five years ago when he first kissed her under the moonlight in Louisville.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On a sweltering summer afternoon, Nick Carraway arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house, where he finds Gatsby waiting nervously; during lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, shocking Tom, who begins to suspect their affair. The group departs for town in a complex car swap—Tom insists on driving Gatsby’s yellow car while Gatsby takes Tom’s blue coupé, with Daisy riding with Gatsby—and en route, they stop at Wilson’s garage, where Tom casually offers to sell Wilson his old car, unaware Wilson has discovered Myrtle’s affair and is emotionally shattered. At the Plaza Hotel, tensions explode as Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and mocks his Oxford claim; Daisy, broken under pressure, admits she once loved both Tom and Gatsby, shattering Gatsby’s idealized dream. Tom orders them to return to Long Island in Gatsby’s car, abandoning them. Later, Myrtle Wilson runs into the road and is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that flees; Michaelis witnesses the aftermath, describing her body with horrific detail—left breast torn loose, mouth ripped—and the car’s color remains uncertain. Tom and Nick arrive at the scene, where Tom immediately denies involvement and shields Wilson from the truth, despite knowing Daisy was driving; after ensuring Wilson is guarded, Tom drives away in tears, calling the driver a coward. That night, Gatsby waits outside the Buchanans’ house, revealing to Nick that Daisy was behind the wheel and he intends to take the blame, while Nick observes Tom and Daisy eating cold chicken together in silent, intimate complicity, realizing Gatsby is guarding nothing but an illusion.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: On the dawn after a sleepless night haunted by a foghorn, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion and finds him dejectedly waiting for Daisy, who had briefly appeared at her window before turning off the light; inside the dusty, opulent house, they search for cigarettes and Gatsby confesses his deception of Daisy during their youthful romance, claiming he falsely presented himself as her social equal and that this fleeting encounter became an all-consuming obsession. Later, in a reflective tone, Nick Carraway recalls Gatsby’s quiet, intimate hour with Daisy on the final afternoon before his departure abroad, where silence and tender gestures replaced words, and Gatsby abandoned grand ambitions for the simple comfort of her presence; after returning from Oxford, penniless and heartbroken, Gatsby traveled by day-coach to Louisville to revisit places tied to Daisy, desperately reaching for the fading memory of her as the train pulled away. Meanwhile, George Wilson, shattered by Myrtle’s death and convinced the yellow car’s driver murdered her, traces the car to Gatsby’s house after spending hours wandering Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, appearing increasingly unhinged; at two o'clock, Gatsby dons his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, and instructs the butler to bring any calls to him by the pool, where he is later found dead, floating on the mattress, moments after Wilson—having arrived at the mansion and fired gunshots—lies dead in the grass, completing the chapter’s tragic holocaust.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is left alone amid a frenzy of media and police at Gatsby’s mansion, where reporters sensationalize Wilson as a 'madman' and Catherine falsely testifies that Myrtle never knew Gatsby; despite desperate attempts to reach Daisy and Meyer Wolfshiem—via phone, letter, and butler—Nick Carraway receives only cold rejections and a mistaken long-distance call implying Gatsby is alive. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, emotionally shattered, and proudly shows Nick a photograph of the mansion and Gatsby’s childhood schedule in a worn copy of Hopalong Cassidy; Nick Carraway tries to summon mourners, but Klipspringer only asks for his tennis shoes and Wolfshiem refuses to attend, citing a personal rule against involvement after death, leaving only Gatz and Nick Carraway at the funeral, where rain falls as the minister speaks. Later, in a thick drizzle, a procession of three cars—motor hearse, limousine with Gatz and Nick Carraway, and a station wagon with servants and the postman—arrives at the cemetery, where the man with owl-eyed glasses, unrecognized by anyone, appears unexpectedly, wipes his rain-soaked glasses, murmurs 'Amen to that' after hearing 'Blessed are the dead that the rain falls on,' and laments that so many once came to Gatsby’s parties but none came to his funeral. Nick Carraway reflects on his Midwest childhood train journeys, defining it by sensory memories of snow, sleigh bells, and holly wreaths, contrasting it with his El Greco-like vision of morally warped East Egg; he visits Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man, and he admits he is too old to call dishonesty honor, ending their relationship with unresolved anger and regret. On a late October afternoon, Nick encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as self-preservation and emotionally manipulating Nick by crying over dog biscuits; Nick shakes his hand, seeing Tom as childlike, before watching him enter a jewelry store to buy a pearl necklace or cuff buttons. Finally, alone at Gatsby’s abandoned mansion, Nick Carraway finds an obscene word scrawled on the white steps, erases it with his shoe, walks to the beach, and meditates on the island’s lost natural beauty, comparing it to Gatsby’s futile pursuit of the green light and the unreachable future, concluding with the metaphor of humanity striving against the current, forever pulled back into the past.

plot_summary.plot_summary:
In the spring of 1922, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg on Long Island, renting a modest home next to the lavish mansion of the enigmatic Jay Gatsby. Through his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom—wealthy, arrogant, and unfaithful—Nick is drawn into the orbit of East Egg’s privileged elite. He quickly becomes entangled in Gatsby’s world after receiving an invitation to one of the millionaire’s extravagant parties, where rumors swirl about Gatsby’s mysterious past. Nick forms a tentative connection with the cynical golf champion Jordan Baker, who later reveals that Gatsby’s entire fortune and estate were built in obsessive pursuit of Daisy, whom he loved five years earlier before being separated by war and class. Gatsby asks Nick to arrange a reunion, hoping to rekindle their romance and erase the intervening years, a dream fueled by his idealized memory of Daisy and the green light across the bay that symbolizes his unattainable longing.

As Gatsby and Daisy rekindle their affair, tensions escalate between Gatsby and Tom, culminating in a violent confrontation at the Plaza Hotel where Tom exposes Gatsby’s criminal ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and ridicules his fabricated Oxford pedigree. Daisy, overwhelmed and conflicted, admits she once loved both men, shattering Gatsby’s illusion that they could return to the past. Later that afternoon, Daisy, driving Gatsby’s yellow car, accidentally kills Myrtle Wilson—Tom’s mistress—in a hit-and-run. Tom manipulates George Wilson, Myrtle’s grief-stricken husband, into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her killer. Meanwhile, Gatsby, still clinging to the hope that Daisy will leave Tom, waits outside her house in vain, taking the blame for the accident. That night, George Wilson, consumed by rage and misinformation, tracks Gatsby to his mansion and shoots him as he floats in his pool, then turns the gun on himself.

In the aftermath, Nick Carraway is left alone to organize Gatsby’s funeral, only to find that the hundreds who once flocked to his parties have vanished. Daisy and Tom retreat into their wealth, leaving no trace of guilt; Meyer Wolfsheim refuses to attend, and Jordan Baker breaks off their relationship, revealing she is engaged to another. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives from Minnesota, proud of his son’s rise despite never knowing the truth behind it. Nick watches as the world moves on, disillusioned by the moral decay beneath the glittering surface of the East. Standing alone at Gatsby’s abandoned mansion, he reflects on the green light and the futile human struggle to recapture the past, concluding that we are all borne back ceaselessly into it. He leaves the East, rejecting its corruption, and returns to the Midwest, forever marked by the tragedy of a man who believed in a dream too beautiful for reality.
